text: Ivan Kliun was born Klyunkov, the son of a carpenter. In 1881 the family moved to Kyiv, seeking to improve their economic condition, and in 1890 they moved again, to Russian Poland. He received his first art education in Warsaw while working as an accountant. In 1898 he relocated to Moscow, where he frequented the studio of Ilya Mashkov, among others. He became a Russian avant-garde painter, sculptor and art theorist of the Suprematist movement.

Giuseppe Bernardino Bison, an itinerant Italian painter, worked on frescoes, landscapes, vedute and capricci. He was born in Palmanova, and as a boy he moved with his family to Brescia, where he saw the works of Girolamo Romani and decided to become a painter. The family then moved to Venice, where he enrolled at the Accademia di Belle Arti and worked with Costantino Cedini. There he became friends with the architect Gian Antonio Selva and went with him to Ferrara in 1787 to help decorate the Palazzo Bottoni.

Nicolas Lancret became a brilliant depicter of light comedy, which reflected the tastes and manners of French society during the regency of the Duke of Orleans and the early reign of Louis XV. Born in Paris, he had Pierre d'Ulin as his first master. His acquaintance with and admiration for Watteau led him to leave Ulin for Gillot, whose pupil Watteau had been. Lancret remained a pupil of Gillot from 1712 to 1713, and the older painter's typical slender figures can be found in many of his early works.

William Henry Prestele is known for the lithographs and watercolor work that the US Department of Agriculture commissioned from him. He was a botanical artist, born in the Grand Duchy of Hesse to Franz Joseph Martin Prestele and Karoline Russ. The family emigrated to America in 1843 and settled first in New York and later in the Amana Colonies in Iowa. His father, known in America as Joseph Prestele, was also a painter.

Theodoor van Thulden is mainly known for his altarpieces, mythological subjects, allegorical works and portraits. He was active in Antwerp, where he had trained, and also in Paris and his native 's-Hertogenbosch. He was baptized Dirrick in St. John's Cathedral there. He was the oldest of at least nine children, and one of his brothers, Franchois, also became a painter. His father was Jacob Gerits van Tulden.

Constantin Guys reported on the Crimean War and drew for British and French newspapers. He was born Ernest-Adolphe Guys de Saint-Hélène in Vlissingen. His father had been appointed civilian chief of the French Navy in Rochefort in 1796 and was stationed in Vlissingen from 1800 until 1805, after which the family moved to Calais. At the age of 20, Constantin served in the cavalry, but only a little later he toured Greece with Lord Byron. He also painted watercolors.

Vladimir Borovikovsky served at the court of Catherine the Great and dominated portraiture in Russia at the turn of the 19th century. He was a Russian artist of Ukrainian Cossack origin, born in Mirgorod, and his father, Luka Borovik, was an icon painter. According to family tradition, all four of Borovik's sons served as Cossacks in the Mirgorod regiment. Vladimir retired early at the rank of poruchik and devoted his life to art, mostly icon painting for local churches.

Elias van Nijmegen is known for ceiling and wall decorations. He was born in Nijmegen, and according to the RKD he became a member of the Leiden Guild of Saint Luke in 1689. Then he moved to Rotterdam, where he married in 1701 and joined the guild the next year. He taught the Rotterdam painters Gerard Sanders and his son Dionys. His daughter Barbara also became a painter. He died in Rotterdam in 1755.

Jan Maurits Quinkhard painted a great number of portraits, and five good examples are in the Amsterdam Museum. He was born in Rees near Cleves and studied with his father, the painter Julius Quinkhardt the Elder, and with Arnold van Boonen. Christoffel Lubinietski and Nikolaas Verkolje were also his teachers. He also painted familiar, allegorical and mythological subjects. His son Julius was instructed by him but abandoned art for commerce.

Jacob Neefs worked on publication projects for prominent Flemish artists of his time, including Rubens, van Dyck and Jacob Jordaens. He was a pupil of Lucas Vorsterman the Elder in Antwerp and was admitted as a master in the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke. In March 1632 he became a member of a fraternity for bachelors established by the Jesuit order. He married Anne Antonissen in 1655.

Pieter van Os was particularly fond of animals as his subject, and he made such an excellent copy of Paulus Potter's Young Bull that William V, Prince of Orange, bought it. He was born in The Hague, the son of Jan van Os, and studied with his father and, from 1794 to 1795, at the Tekenakademie in The Hague. During that time he copied paintings by Paulus Potter and Karel Dujardin. He then left for Amsterdam. He was a Dutch painter and engraver and belonged to the well-known Van Os family of artists.

Karl Nordström specialized in landscapes. From 1896 to 1920 he was chairman of the Association of Artists, Konstnärsförbundet. His father was a police commissioner, and he grew up in Stenkyrka Parish on the island of Tjörn until he was twenty, when he went to Stockholm to study at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts. His primary instructor there was Edvard Perséus. For two years he studied on his own in France, visited museums in Antwerp and Brussels, and became influenced by Impressionism.

Giovanni Battista Foggini, a sculptor active in Florence, is known mainly for small bronze statuary. The Medici Grand Duke of Tuscany sent him to Rome to join the so-called Accademia Fiorentina and to apprentice in the studio of Ercole Ferrata, a pupil of Algardi. The Accademia's first director, Ciro Ferri, also tutored him in drawing. Returning to Florence in 1676, he became the court sculptor for Cosimo III.

Giovanni Bellini is probably the best known of the Bellini family of Venetian painters. He was raised in the household of Jacopo Bellini, whom people formerly thought to be his father, though that relationship is now questioned. An older brother or perhaps nephew, Gentile Bellini, was more highly regarded than Giovanni during their lifetimes, but the reverse is true today. His brother-in-law was Andrea Mantegna. His use of clear, slow-drying oil paints had a great effect on the Venetian painting school, especially on his pupils Giorgione and Titian.

Paul Huet studied under Gros and Guérin. He met the English painter Richard Parkes Bonington in the studio of Gros, where he studied irregularly from 1819 to 1822. Bonington's example led Huet to reject neoclassicism and paint landscapes based on close observation of nature. The British landscape paintings shown in the Salon of 1824 were a revelation to him. Of Constable's work he said it was the first time perhaps that one felt the freshness of a luxuriant, verdant nature, without blackness, crudity or mannerism.

Luca Cambiaso was the leading artist in Genoa in the 16th century. He is considered the founder of the Genoese school, which established the local tradition of historical fresco painting through his many decorations of Genoese churches and palaces. He produced a number of poetic night scenes. He was a prolific draughtsman who sometimes reduced figures to geometric, even cubic, forms. He was familiarly known as Lucchetto da Genova. He was born in Moneglia.

Giovanni Giacometti was the father of the artists Alberto and Diego Giacometti and of the architect Bruno Giacometti. He was the fourth of eight children, and his father, Alberto, was a baker who also ran a café. The painter Augusto Giacometti was his cousin. He received his primary education in Chur, where he developed an interest in art by observing the sculptures at the Bianchi marble works. From 1886 to 1887 he studied at the Kunstgewerbeschule in Munich, since he had wanted to attend the Academy of Fine Arts but was insufficiently prepared.

Richard Houston, born in Dublin about 1721, became a pupil of John Brooks, who was also the master of James McArdell and Charles Spooner. He came to London about 1747, and some of his early plates bear the address near Drummond's at Charing Cross. In debt to the print-seller Robert Sayer, he was arrested and confined to the Fleet prison. He was released in 1760, on the accession of George III. As a free agent he was commissioned by Henry Carrington Bowles. He was an Irish mezzotint engraver.

Eugène Galien-Laloue made himself a populariser of street scenes, usually painted in autumn or winter. He was born in Paris of French-Italian parents. His paintings of the early 1900s show Paris in la Belle Époque, a happy, bustling city with horse-drawn carriages, trolley cars and its first omnibuses. His works are valued for their contribution to 20th-century art and for the actual history they document. His work can be seen at the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Louviers and La Rochelle, and in Mulhouse.

Rudolf Swoboda the Younger was sometimes called that to distinguish him from his uncle Rudolf, who was also an artist. He painted Orientalist subjects. He studied under his father, Eduard Swoboda, and his uncle Leopold Carl Müller, and travelled with Müller to Egypt in 1880. His sister Josefine was a portrait painter, also well known for her portraits of the British royal family. In 1886 Queen Victoria commissioned him to paint several of a group of Indian artisans who had been brought to Windsor Castle.

Gilliam van der Gouwen is known for reproductive engravings and for title pages, maps and book illustrations for the Amsterdam publishers. He was born in Antwerp around 1657. In the guild year 1669–1670 he was registered at the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke, studying engraving as a pupil of Pieter van Lisebetten. There is no record of him registering as a master in the Antwerp Guild. He left Antwerp and spent most of his active career in the Dutch Republic.

Hermann Kern was one of the most popular Austrian genre painters of his time and a court painter to Franz Josef I in Vienna. He was born into a noble family in Liptóújvár, now Liptovský Hrádok in Slovakia. His father, a famous doctor, Benjamin von Kern, recognized his exceptional talent early and paid for his education. Kern began his artistic training at sixteen in Levoča under Theo Böhm. In 1854 he went to Prague, where he studied under Klemens, and then attended the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna.

Arthur Dove is often considered the first American abstract painter. He was an early American modernist who used a wide range of media, sometimes in unconventional combinations, to produce his abstractions and abstract landscapes. Me and the Moon from 1937 is a good example of his abstract landscapes and has been referred to as one of the culminating works of his career. He made a series of experimental collages in the 1920s. He also experimented with techniques, combining paints like hand-mixed oil or tempera over a wax emulsion.

Cherubino Alberti, also called Borghegiano, is most often remembered for the Roman frescoes he completed with his brother Giovanni during the papacy of Clement VIII. He was most prolific as an engraver of copper plates. He was born in Borgo San Sepolcro into a family of artists, the second son of Alberto Alberti, a carver and sculptor. His brothers Alessandro and Giovanni were artists as well. Alberti studied in Rome under Cornelius Cort and worked as an engraver.

Constantin Hansen belonged to the Golden Age of Danish painting. He was deeply interested in literature and mythology, and the art historian Niels Laurits Høyen inspired him to try to recreate a national historical painting based on Norse mythology. He painted many altarpieces and portraits, including the monumental oil painting The Danish Constituent Assembly, made between 1861 and 1865. He was born in Rome, the son of the portrait painter Hans Hansen. The family soon relocated to Vienna.

Jacob de Wet II is known for a series of 110 portraits of Scottish monarchs, many of them mythical, produced for the Palace of Holyroodhouse in Edinburgh during the reign of Charles II. According to the RKD, he was one of five children of the painter Jacob Willemszoon de Wet. His father taught him to paint, and he was first recorded in his father's notebook at the age of sixteen, when his father wrote that he had sold one of his son's paintings. In 1668 he moved to Amsterdam and married Helena Stalmans.

Wilhelm Busch published wildly innovative illustrated tales that remain influential to this day. He drew on the tropes of folk humour and on a deep knowledge of German literature to satirize contemporary life, piety, Catholicism and Philistinism. His mastery of drawing and verse influenced generations of comic artists and vernacular poets. The Katzenjammer Kids was inspired by his Max and Moritz. He was a German humorist and painter.

Laurent de La Hyre, born in Paris, was a leading exponent of the neoclassical style of Parisian Atticism. The work of Italian artists who came to Paris influenced him greatly. He never visited Italy. He became a pupil of Georges Lallemand and studied the works of Primaticcio at Fontainebleau. His use of color and delicately posed figures are a trademark of his early style. He was an innovative artist who used his skills as a storyteller to portray rarely depicted subjects.

Johannes Gijsbert Vogel, a Dutch landscape painter, was born in Hooge Zwaluwe, the son of the local mayor, and moved to The Hague, where he became a pupil of Andreas Schelfhout. He became a member of Pulchri Studio and married Maria Henrietta Catherina van Wielik in 1854. After she died, he remarried the painter Margaretha Roosenboom, the granddaughter of his teacher Schelfhout. After her death he married a third time in 1902. His brother Hugo Pieter Vogel was an architect.

Johann Georg Platzer came from a family of painters in Eppan, in the County of Tyrol. He painted primarily historical and mythical scenes. The Joanneum Alte Galerie in Graz houses the largest collection of his work under a single roof. He worked with his uncle as a court painter in Passau. Then he returned to Eppan, where he kept working until his death in 1761. He was a prolific Austrian Rococo painter and draughtsman.

Henri Gaudier-Brzeska developed a rough-hewn, primitive style of direct carving. He was a French artist and sculptor, born Gaudier in Saint-Jean-de-Braye near Orléans. In 1910 he moved to London to become an artist, even though he had no formal training. With him came Sophie Brzeska, a Polish writer 19 years his senior whom he had met at the Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève in Paris. They began an intense relationship, and he added her surname to his own, though they never married.

Adalbert Volck worked as a dentist but became best known for his political cartoons in support of the Confederacy during the American Civil War. He was born in Augsburg and lived for most of his life in Baltimore. He has been described as the Northern art world's most famous Confederate sympathizer. His support extended beyond his cartoons. He smuggled items for the Confederate army and acted as a personal courier for President Jefferson Davis.

Moses ter Borch died in battle during one of the Dutch fleet's engagements in England during the Second Anglo-Dutch War. His surviving work consists mostly of drawings. He was born in Zwolle, the youngest son of Gerard ter Borch the Elder and Wiesken Matthys. His father had initially been a painter but had changed careers to become a convoy and license master in Zwolle. Moses's elder siblings included his half-brother, the prominent painter Gerard ter Borch.

George Clausen worked in oil and watercolour. He also made etchings and mezzotints. The Crown knighted him in 1927. He was born in the Regents Park district of London, the son of a decorative artist of Danish descent and a Scottish mother. From 1867 to 1873 he attended design classes at the South Kensington Schools with great success. He then worked in the studio of Edwin Long and later in Paris at the Académie Julian, under Bouguereau and Tony Robert-Fleury.

Anne Rushout painted watercolours, many of them botanical studies, and kept a diary. She was the eldest daughter of John Rushout, 1st Baron Northwick, and his wife Rebecca, born Bowles. Anne never married. Her sisters and one of her brothers did marry, but her other brother, John Rushout, 2nd Baron Northwick, did not. She and John lived together for many years. Other artists of her time painted her as well.

Léon Bonnat lived in Madrid from 1846 to 1853, where his father owned a bookshop. While tending the shop, he copied engravings of works by the Old Masters and developed a passion for drawing. In Madrid he received his artistic training under Madrazo. He later worked in Paris, where he became known as a leading portraitist, never without a commission. Velázquez and Ribera influenced his portraits. He was also an art collector and a professor at the Ecole des Beaux Arts.

Edmund Blair Leighton painted historical genre scenes, specialising in Regency and medieval subjects. His art is linked to the Pre-Raphaelite movement, though it is less stylised and much more naturalistic. He was the son of the artist Charles Blair Leighton. He was educated at University College School. At fifteen he left to work for a tea merchant. Wishing to study art, he went to evening classes in South Kensington and then to the Heatherley School.

Frederick Arthur Bridgman, an American artist, is known for his paintings of Orientalist subjects. He was born in Tuskegee, Alabama, the son of a physician. After his father died in 1850, his mother moved to New York City with her two sons. In 1864 he began working as a draughtsman for the American Bank Note Company, and in the same years he studied art at the Brooklyn Art Association.

Born Jean-Joseph Constant in Paris, Benjamin-Constant became a French painter and etcher best known for his Oriental subjects and portraits. He studied at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Toulouse, where he was a pupil of Alexandre Cabanel. A journey to Morocco in 1872 strongly influenced his early artistic development and led him to produce Romantic scenes under the spell of Orientalism. Among his noted works in this vein are Last Rebels and Justice in the Harem, both in the Luxembourg Gallery.

William Stanley Haseltine belonged to the Düsseldorf school of painting, the Hudson River School and Luminism. He was born in Philadelphia to the businessman John Haseltine and Elizabeth Shinn Haseltine, an amateur landscape painter. He studied at the University of Pennsylvania and then at Harvard University, where he received a degree in 1854. The following year he first exhibited his paintings at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. After that he sailed to Europe.

William Chambers designed Somerset House, the Gold State Coach and the pagoda at Kew. He was a Swedish-born British architect and a founder member of the Royal Academy. He was born in Gothenburg to a Scottish merchant father. Between 1740 and 1749 he was employed by the Swedish East India Company, making three voyages to China, where he studied Chinese architecture and decoration. During that employment he befriended David af Sandeberg, the company's director.

Henry Moret is best known for his part in the Pont-Aven artist colony and for his richly colored landscapes of coastal Brittany. He was a French Impressionist painter, among those who gathered around Paul Gauguin at Pont-Aven. He was born in Cherbourg, but little is known of his life until his military service began in 1875. His commander in Lorient, Jules La Villette, first noticed his artistic talent and introduced him to Ernest Corroller, a drawing teacher and marine painter, who taught him landscape painting.

Benjamin Williams Leader, a British landscape painter, started life as Benjamin Leader Williams, the third of eleven children of the civil engineer Edward Leader Williams. His father was a keen amateur artist and a friend of John Constable, and Benjamin would often accompany him on sketching trips. His father was described as a non-conformist dissenter, and his mother, Sarah Whiting, was a Quaker. Their marriage in an Anglican church resulted in them being disowned by the Society of Friends.

Gerrit Lamberts became curator of the museum in Amsterdam in 1825, when it was housed in the Trippenhuis. He was born in Amsterdam and started out as a paper merchant. Later he became a watercolorist, draughtsman and engraver. He is known for topographic drawings of cityscapes, architectural views of buildings and watercolors of art galleries. He was also a bookseller. He was a member of the Amsterdam academy, which was housed in the same building.

After the start of his career, Melchior d'Hondecoeter painted virtually exclusively bird subjects, usually exotic birds or game, in park-like landscapes. His paintings featured geese, ducks and peacocks, and also exotic birds such as sarus cranes and yellow-crested cockatoos. He was a Dutch animal painter, born in Utrecht, who died in Amsterdam. He was the grandson of the painter Gillis d'Hondecoeter.

Raimundo de Madrazo y Garreta belonged to the Madrazo family of Spanish artists. He was born in Rome into a family of artists with a noble background. His grandfather José de Madrazo was a painter and former director of the Museo del Prado, and his father, Federico de Madrazo, was a portrait painter. He worked in the Realistic style, although his later work shows signs of Rococo and Japanese influence. He was known primarily for his genre paintings and portraits.

Cornelis van Poelenburgh was the leading representative of the first generation of Dutch landscape painters who were active in Rome in the early 17th century. He was known for small-scale paintings of Italianate landscapes with small figures enacting biblical or mythological scenes or in contemporary attire. His birthplace is unknown. A signed document survives in Utrecht listing him as six years old and the son of Simon van Poelenburch, a Catholic canon. He initially trained with Abraham Bloemaert.

Adrianus Eversen portrayed the typical 19th-century Dutch atmosphere in his work. As a member of Arti et Amicitiae, he belonged to the society of elite artists of his time. He was a contemporary of Cornelis Springer, and both were students of Hendrik Gerrit ten Cate at the same time and usually painted contemporary regional cityscapes. In his choice of subjects Eversen allowed himself more freedom. He painted mostly imaginary cityscapes, made of existing and invented fragments, unlike Springer's more faithful representations.

Albert Pinkham Ryder is best known for his poetic and moody allegorical works and seascapes, as well as for his eccentric personality. His art shared an emphasis on subtle variations of color with the tonalist works of the time, but it accentuated form in a way that some art historians regard as a precursor to modernism. He was born in New Bedford, Massachusetts, a bustling whaling port that probably supplied artistic inspiration with its intimate connection to the sea. He was the youngest of four children.

Fanny Churberg was the third of seven children, born in Vaasa. Her father, Matias, was a doctor from a family of farmers, and her mother, Maria, was the daughter of the vicar of Liperi parish. Four of her siblings died young, so Fanny grew up with her two older brothers. She was proud of her Ostrobothnian family and heritage, and she planned with her brothers to change the surname to Kuurila, after the family's old estate. She became a Finnish landscape painter.

Vilhelm Kyhn belonged to the generation of national romantic painters who came right after the Danish Golden Age and before the Modern Breakthrough. He outlived many of his artistic peers by several decades but remained a traditionalist and strongly criticised many of the new trends in painting. He also worked as an educator and established several alternative art schools, among them a painting school for women that Anna Ancher attended. He was a Danish landscape painter, born in Copenhagen.

Louis Rhead grew up in a family that had worked in the Staffordshire Potteries for at least three generations. His father, George W. Rhead, was a highly respected gilder and ceramic artist. In the 1870s George taught art and design in Staffordshire schools and founded the Fenton School of Art. Louis and all his siblings attended their father's art classes. He emigrated to the United States at the age of twenty-four and worked as an artist and illustrator.

Pieter Quast grew up near the Zeedijk in Amsterdam, the son of a barge master from Emden. In 1632 he promised to marry Annetje Splinters, a flower painter from The Hague. She sued him for breaking his vows. Half a year later she forced him to marry her. They moved to The Hague, where he was admitted to the local Guild of Saint Luke in 1634. He worked as a painter, draughtsman of portraits and sculptor.

Charles Baugniet is remembered for his lithographed portraits of famous and lesser-known figures. His sitters came from several countries and included politicians and clergy. Others were professors and artists. He was a Belgian painter, lithographer and aquarellist. He was born in Brussels and attended the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts there in 1827–29, where he studied under Joseph Paelinck and Florent Willems.

Giovanni di Paolo worked primarily in Siena and became a prolific painter and illustrator of manuscripts, including Dante's texts. His early works show the influence of earlier Sienese masters, but his later style was more individual, with cold, harsh colours and elongated forms. International Gothic artists such as Gentile da Fabriano also influenced his style. Many of his works have an unusual dreamlike atmosphere, such as the surrealistic Miracle of Saint Nicholas of Tolentino.

Hugo Kauffmann was the son of the painter Hermann Kauffmann. In 1861 he went to Frankfurt, where he worked under Jakob Becker, Eduard Jakob von Steinle and Johann Nepomuk Zwerger. He then lived in Kronberg in the Taunus, with a winter in Hamburg, five months in Düsseldorf and a year and a half in Paris, until the war drove him out in 1870. He lived in Munich until 1871. Kauffmann is known mainly for genre paintings, often set in taverns. They are usually small and painted on wood.

Caspar Netscher painted oriental rugs, silk and brocade so well that he introduced an international style to the Northern Netherlands. According to Houbraken, he was born in Heidelberg or Prague. His father, Johann Netscher, was a sculptor from Stuttgart who married Elizabet Vetter, the daughter of a mayor of Heidelberg, against her father's wishes. He died in Poland when Caspar was two years old. It has been suggested that Caspar may have been the son of a Rotterdam painter.

Bernhard Rode was well known for portraying historical scenes and allegorical works. He knew most of the central figures of the Berlin Enlightenment, such as Friedrich Nicolai and Gotthold Lessing, and their philosophical and political discussions informed much of the subject matter of his work. His paintings include several works depicting Frederick the Great in various guises. He was director of the Berlin Academy of the Arts from 1783 until his death in 1797. He was a Prussian artist and engraver.

At the age of eight, James Jebusa Shannon was taken by his parents from Auburn, New York, where he was born, to Canada. When he was sixteen, he went to England, where he studied at South Kensington, and after three years he won the gold medal for figure painting. His portrait of the Hon. Horatia Stopford, one of the queen's maids of honour, attracted attention at the Royal Academy in 1881. In 1886 he married Florence Mary Cartwright, and their only child was the illustrator Kitty Shannon.

Leendert de Koningh was a Dutch marine and landscape painter, instructed by Vermeulen and Versteeg. In 1801 he came to England, but in 1803 the War of the Third Coalition forced him to leave. He then studied under David in Paris and returned through Germany to his hometown of Dordrecht, where he spent the rest of his life. He paid a second visit to England in 1816.

Solon Borglum is most noted for his depiction of frontier life, and especially for his experience with cowboys and Native Americans. He was an American sculptor. France awarded him the Croix de Guerre for his work with the Foyers du Soldat service clubs during World War I. He was born in Ogden, Utah, the younger brother of Gutzon Borglum and the uncle of Lincoln Borglum, the two men most responsible for the carvings at Mount Rushmore. His Danish immigrant father, James, was a Mormon polygamist married to two sisters.

Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach's Baroque architecture shaped the tastes of the Habsburg Empire. His book A Plan of Civil and Historical Architecture, published in 1721, was one of the first and most popular comparative studies of world architecture. His major works include Schönbrunn Palace and the Karlskirche in Vienna and the Kollegienkirche in Salzburg. He was an Austrian architect and sculptor, born in Graz.

Antoine Pesne started in the baroque manner and became one of the fathers of rococo in painting. He was born in Paris and first studied art under his father and uncle. From 1704 to 1710 he received a stipend for advanced training at the Académie Royale in Italy. In 1710 King Frederick I in Prussia called him to Berlin. The king had seen and liked a painting of a German nobleman that Pesne had completed in Venice. He became court painter.

Charles-Nicolas Cochin studied engraving under his father, Charles-Nicolas Cochin the Elder, which is why he is called the Younger. He is also called Cochin le fils, or Cochin II. His mother, Louise-Magdeleine Horthemels, was herself an important engraver in Paris for some fifty years. Beyond his artistic education, Cochin taught himself Latin, English and Italian. He was born in Paris. He worked as a French engraver and art critic.

Cornelis Danckerts the Elder worked in Amsterdam as a publisher, printer and engraver. He was the oldest of at least five children of Danckert Corneliszn., a skipper, and Lijsbeth Jansd., who married in 1603. In 1633 he married Anneken van Minne in the Hooglandse kerk in Leiden. At that time he worked as a paper and map seller in Amsterdam. They had at least six children together.

Christian Fritzsch was the son of a shepherd in Saxony and received his first training from Martin Bernigeroth in Leipzig. He then moved to Hamburg to join his friend, the portrait painter Johann Salomon Wahl, who also came from Saxony and supplied portraits to the Danish royal court from there. Fritzsch received Hamburg citizenship on 8 April 1718. He became court engraver to Duke Karl Friedrich of Holstein-Gottorp, who gave him a country house in Schiffbek, which became the centre of his life.

Gerardus Johannes Bos grew up on the Breestraat in Leiden, the son of the watchmaker Christiaan Bos and his wife Johanna Maria Domus. He studied with Hendrik Langelaan and Cornet. He worked as a painter, etcher, lithographer and printer. He married twice, and his first wife died in 1885. He lived on the Rapenburg and died in Leiden in 1898.

Ľudovít Čordák grew up in a tailor's family of Polish-Ukrainian origin and studied at the gymnasium in Košice under Vojtech Klimkovič. In 1883 he began to attend the teacher training school for drawing in Budapest. He moved with his parents to Munich, where he lived for six years. From 1889 to 1895 he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague, in Julius Mařák's school of landscape painting. After graduating he returned to Slovakia and settled first in Turňa nad Bodvou and later in Košice.

Carl von Hasenauer, an Austrian architect of historicism, designed the Natural History Museum, the Art History Museum, the New Burgtheater and the Neue Hofburg in Vienna together with his German colleague Gottfried Semper. He also designed further buildings in Vienna on his own. Because of his neo-Baroque style he was nicknamed the building Makart. He was born in Vienna and became a baron in 1873. He died there in 1894.

Philipp Rumpf learned the confectioner's trade from his father, the son of a confectioner in Frankfurt. In 1836 he began studying sculpture under Johann Nepomuk Zwerger at the Städel Institute. Later he studied painting with Jakob Becker, Carl Friedrich Wendelstadt, Heinrich von Rustige and Jakob Fürchtegott Dielmann. In 1844 he founded an art school for the daughters of the bourgeoisie. In 1852 he visited Paris, where he saw the works of Camille Corot and Gustave Courbet. He worked as a painter and etcher.

Simon Andreas Krausz studied with Léonard Defrance and later at the academy in The Hague. In 1780 he became a member of Confrerie Pictura, and in 1782 he won a gold medal. He mostly painted landscapes and interiors. He lived and worked in The Hague and taught Hendrikus van de Sande Bakhuyzen and Frederik Lodewijk Huygens. The Rijksmuseum owns about 130 of his drawings and paintings, from careful studies to loose sketches of peasant life, and twenty etchings.

Edmond Morin, a French painter, illustrator and engraver, studied under Charles Gleyre at the École des beaux-arts in Paris. After the coup d'état of 2 December 1851 he spent five years in London, working for The Illustrated London News, where he befriended the engravers William James Linton and his brother Henry Duff. He then returned to Paris with Henry. There he worked for La Vie parisienne and Le Monde illustré, becoming one of the latter's principal illustrators alongside Albert Duvivier and Charles-Théodore Sauvageot.
